title: Vaginal Discharge - Diagnosis and Management of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
patient_instructions: You are Chloe, a 25-year-old hospitality worker. You have had an abnormal vaginal discharge for about a week - yellowish, and it smells unpleasant. You also have a dull lower abdominal/pelvic ache and have felt a bit feverish. If asked sensitively: you have had two new partners in the last few months, you do not always use condoms, and you were treated for chlamydia about a year ago. You have some pain during deep sex but no bleeding after sex and no bleeding between periods. Your last period was normal and about two weeks ago. You feel a bit nauseated but have not vomited. No urinary burning. You take no regular medications, use no tampons currently, and are on no contraceptive pill. You are up to date with nothing (cervical screening starts at 25 and you have not booked). IDEAS: 'Maybe it is just thrush.' CONCERNS: 'Could this affect my ability to have children?' EXPECTATIONS: to get treated. Affect: embarrassed about the sexual history, cooperative if approached without judgement. On the screen: examination shows yellowish discharge, cervical motion tenderness, a tender uterus and tender adnexae on bimanual examination; urine pregnancy test negative.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP. Chloe, 25, presents with abnormal vaginal discharge. Examination findings are on the screen (yellow discharge, cervical motion tenderness, tender uterus and adnexae, negative pregnancy test). In 8 minutes: take a focused history including a sexual history, state your provisional diagnosis and differentials, and outline your investigations and management including empirical treatment and safety-netting.
examiner_instructions: The candidate should take a structured discharge history (timing, colour/consistency/volume/odour, itch/pain/dysuria) and a sensitive, permission-based sexual history, and screen not-to-be-missed causes (PID, cervical cancer, ovarian pathology, ectopic). Given yellow offensive discharge, pelvic pain, fever, cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness with multiple partners and prior chlamydia, the diagnosis is pelvic inflammatory disease. Expect swabs (endocervical/self-collected NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea/trichomonas, high vaginal swab, gonococcal culture for susceptibility), a full STI screen (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C), and empirical eTG treatment started before results: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM PLUS doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days PLUS metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days. Reward contact tracing, safe-sex advice and safety-netting for tubo-ovarian abscess/sepsis. Prompt if needed: 'What antibiotics would you start today?'

criteria: Characterises the discharge (timing, colour, volume, odour, associated itch/pain/dysuria)
Takes a sensitive, permission-based sexual history (partners, condom use, prior STIs, practices)
Screens PID and cancer red flags (fever, pelvic pain, postcoital/intermenstrual bleeding, weight loss, bloating)
Uses a non-judgemental, empathic approach and elicits concerns (fertility)
Diagnoses pelvic inflammatory disease from discharge, pelvic pain, fever, cervical motion and adnexal tenderness
Gives an appropriate differential (STIs, BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, cervical pathology, ovarian, physiological)
Links prior chlamydia and multiple partners as risk factors and excludes pregnancy/ectopic
Orders swabs (CT/NG/TV NAAT, high vaginal swab, gonococcal culture) and a full STI screen and Cervical Screening Test
Starts empirical eTG PID therapy: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days plus metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days
Arranges contact tracing/partner notification, safe-sex advice and safety-netting for tubo-ovarian abscess/sepsis and infertility risk
Explains the diagnosis and plan sensitively in lay terms and checks understanding

red_flags: Pelvic pain with fever, cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness - PID progressing to tubo-ovarian abscess or sepsis requires admission and IV antibiotics
Postmenopausal bleeding or blood-stained discharge - endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, mandating transvaginal ultrasound +/- pipelle/hysteroscopy
Cervical mass/ulceration, friable cervix bleeding on contact, or postcoital bleeding - urgent gynaecology referral for suspected cervical cancer
Positive pregnancy test with pelvic pain - exclude ectopic pregnancy
Long-term PID sequelae: infertility, chronic pelvic pain and increased ectopic risk
australian_guidelines: eTG (Antibiotic) empirical PID regimen: ceftriaxone 500 mg (in 2 mL of 1% lignocaine) IM as a single dose PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally BD for 14 days PLUS metronidazole 400 mg orally BD for 14 days; treat before swab results
eTG trichomoniasis: metronidazole 400 mg orally 12-hourly for 7 days (preferred) or 2 g orally as a single dose (alternative); treat partners and note it is a notifiable STI in several jurisdictions
eTG recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis: fluconazole 150 mg orally on days 1, 4 and 7 (induction) then 150 mg once weekly for 6 months (maintenance); confirm species on culture and screen for diabetes

Australian STI practice: self- or clinician-collected vaginal swab for CT/NG/TV NAAT plus gonococcal culture for susceptibility, full STI screen (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C), contact tracing; National Cervical Screening Program uses HPV-based testing from age 25 every 5 years
learning_objectives: Take a structured discharge and sensitive sexual history
Diagnose PID clinically and differentiate it from other causes of discharge
Order appropriate STI investigations and start empirical eTG therapy before results
Arrange contact tracing, safe-sex advice and safety-netting for complications
key_points: Start empirical PID treatment on clinical grounds before swab results - do not wait
Perform gonococcal culture (not just NAAT) where possible for antimicrobial susceptibility
Any postmenopausal blood-stained discharge is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise
Counsel on long-term PID sequelae - infertility, chronic pelvic pain and ectopic pregnancy risk

citations.claim: Cervical malignancy must be excluded in vaginal discharge (offensive discharge, ulceration/mass, friable cervix), and postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2547

citations.claim: A focal lesion on the vulva should always be biopsied - relevant to the dermatological/neoplastic differentials of discharge.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2645

citations.claim: Ovarian pathology is a differential to consider when discharge is accompanied by bloating and pelvic symptoms.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2564
